doc.summary: Framework for Reusable Organized Data Output
doc.description:
One tool to rule them all, one tool to find them.

FRODO manages, organises and archives CFD simulation data across
multiple formats, forging results into a unified structure ready for
analysis, plotting, or machine learning.

A FRODO instance is a thin coordinator: on construction it builds a
quartet of format-specific helpers (``reader``, ``sets``,
``residuals``, ``stats``) from the registries, and then forwards
unknown attribute lookups to them via :meth:`__getattr__`. Most of
what callers invoke as ``db.something(...)`` therefore lives on one of
those four objects, not on FRODO. The only heavyweight logic FRODO
owns is :meth:`merge_datasets`.

attributes.name: format
attributes.desc: The format key used to select the quartet from the registries.

attributes.name: root_dir
attributes.desc: Absolute path to the database root (``os.path.abspath`` applied).

attributes.name: reader
attributes.desc: Format-specific parser. Always present.

attributes.name: sets
attributes.desc: Tensor/mesh/IO helper, or ``None`` when the format registers no Sets class (HORSES3D; also CODA and NUMPY when pyLOM is missing).

attributes.name: residuals
attributes.desc: Convergence helper, or ``None`` (NUMPY, NUMPYFILE, PYLOM).

attributes.name: stats
attributes.desc: Statistics helper, or ``None`` (NUMPYFILE, PYLOM, HORSES3D).

attributes.name: sim_metadata
attributes.desc: Per-case metadata collected by the reader while parsing.

attributes.name: df_state
attributes.desc: One row per case describing its state on disk. Created by :meth:`_parse`, so absent when ``initial_parse=False``.

attributes.name: data_dict
attributes.desc: The extracted data. Empty until :meth:`extract_inputs` / :meth:`extract_outputs` run. Its layout is format-dependent.

attributes.name: name
attributes.desc: Human-readable label. Defaults to ``'FRODO Database'``.

attributes.name: kwargs
attributes.desc: The extra keyword arguments forwarded to the reader constructor, kept so that :meth:`copy` can rebuild the quartet.

attributes.name: update_df_state
attributes.desc: Whether the reader should refresh ``df_state`` while extracting.

text_sections.title: Supported formats
text_sections.text:
Determined at runtime from ``READER_REGISTRY``. Currently 'CODA',
'CODA_SINGLE', 'NUMPY', 'NUMPYFILE', 'PYLOM' and 'HORSES3D'. Not
every format provides all four pieces; see the module docstring for
the availability matrix.

text_sections.title: Notes
text_sections.text:
``db.metadata`` is **not** an attribute of FRODO. It resolves through
:meth:`__getattr__` to ``reader.metadata``, which is where
``df_cases``, ``design_vars``, ``eq_type``, ``folder_fmt`` and
``num_stages`` live. The exception is instances produced by
:meth:`copy` and :meth:`merge_datasets`, which set ``metadata`` as a
real attribute on the new object; there, FRODO's own copy shadows the
reader's. Code that mutates ``db.metadata`` should be aware of which
of the two it is holding.

text_sections.title: Examples
text_sections.text:
Open a CODA database and extract one CAD group::

    from FotR import FRODO

    db = FRODO(root_dir='/data/TIFON', format='CODA', name='tifon')
    db.extract_inputs(id_group='3')
    db.extract_outputs(id_group='3', stage='all')
    db.summary_data()

The quartet is reachable both directly and by delegation::

    db.sets.add_aux(...)   # explicit
    db.add_aux(...)        # same call, resolved by __getattr__

doc.summary: Shortcut to Eärendil's Light help system.
Resolve an unknown attribute against the format quartet.
doc.description:
If FRODO itself has no attribute *name*, the four sub-objects are
searched **in this fixed order**: ``sets``, ``reader``,
``residuals``, ``stats``. The first one that has the attribute
wins. This lets callers write ``db.add_aux(...)`` when the method
actually lives on ``db.sets``, without FRODO having to re-export
anything.

params.name: name
params.desc: Attribute being looked up.

returns.desc: The attribute taken from the first sub-object that has it.

raises.desc: If none of the four sub-objects provides *name*.

text_sections.title: Notes
text_sections.text:
Three consequences worth knowing before relying on delegation:

* **Python only calls this when normal lookup fails.** The real
  attributes of the instance (``format``, ``root_dir``,
  ``sim_metadata``, ``data_dict``, ``df_state``, ``name``,
  ``kwargs``, ``update_df_state``, and the quartet itself) are
  never delegated.
* **The same call can have a different signature per format.**
  ``db.extract_inputs`` reaches ``CODAReader.extract_inputs`` in
  one database and ``NUMPYReader.extract_inputs`` in another;
  argument names and order are not guaranteed to match. When in
  doubt, read the docstring of the concrete reader/sets class
  rather than of FRODO.
* **Name collisions are resolved by the order above, silently.**
  ``db.summary`` reaches ``sets.summary`` even though readers also
  define one, and ``db.db`` reaches ``sets.db`` (the back-pointer
  each sets/stats/residuals object keeps to its parent FRODO), not
  anything of FRODO's own. Address the sub-object explicitly
  (``db.reader.summary``) when the distinction matters.

doc.summary: Instantiate the reader/sets/residuals/stats quartet from the registries.
doc.description:
The reader receives ``root_dir=...`` plus the leftover
``**kwargs``; sets, residuals and stats receive only ``db=self``,
the back-pointer they use to reach the parsed data.

Registry values of None mean "format known but submodule not yet
implemented"; a ``UserWarning`` is emitted and the attribute is set
to None. A missing key in ``READER_REGISTRY`` raises ``ValueError``.

doc.summary: Build a hashable identity key for a single case from its design-variable values.

params.name: row
params.desc: Design-variable values for one case (one row of ``FlCc`` or of a design-variable-indexed DataFrame).

params.name: decimals
params.desc: Number of decimal places used to round the values before hashing.  This defines the numerical precision at which two cases are considered "the same physical case" — see the ``dedup_decimals`` parameter of :meth:`merge_datasets`.

returns.desc: Rounded, hashable identity key.

text_sections.title: Examples
text_sections.text:
::

    key = FRODO._case_identity_key(np.array([3.00000001, 0.75]), 6)
    # (3.0, 0.75)

doc.summary: Verify that no two sources contain the same physical case.
doc.description:
Every row of every source's ``FlCc`` is turned into an identity
key via :meth:`_case_identity_key`; if the same key is produced by
two different sources (or twice within the same source), a
``ValueError`` is raised immediately, naming both offending
sources and row positions.

This function deliberately does **not** deduplicate: the design
philosophy of :meth:`merge_datasets` is "different cases →
concatenate, duplicate cases → error", never "duplicate cases →
silently keep one".

params.name: flcc_by_source
params.desc: One ``FlCc`` array (shape ``(n_cases, n_dvars)``) per source, in the same order as ``source_labels``.

params.name: decimals
params.desc: Rounding precision used to build identity keys — see ``dedup_decimals`` in :meth:`merge_datasets`.

params.name: source_labels
params.desc: Human-readable label per source (e.g. ``'source 0'``), used only for the error message.

raises.desc: On the first duplicate found.

text_sections.title: Examples
text_sections.text:
::

    FRODO._check_no_duplicate_cases(
        [flcc_a, flcc_b], decimals=8,
        source_labels=['source 0', 'source 1'],
    )

methods.name: _match_rows_by_identity
methods.signature: _match_rows_by_identity(flcc: np.ndarray, design_vars: list, reference_df: pd.DataFrame, decimals: int, context: str)

doc.summary: Reorder (and filter) a case-indexed DataFrame so that its rows correspond, one-to-one and in order, to the extracted cases in ``flcc``.
doc.description:
For every row of ``flcc`` this looks up the single matching row of
``reference_df`` — matched on ``design_vars`` values, rounded to
``decimals`` places — and returns those rows stitched back
together in ``flcc``'s row order. This is the mechanism that keeps
``df_state`` / ``df_post`` synchronised with the cases that were
*actually extracted* (``FlCc``) instead of accidentally including
every case merely *defined* in the source database.

params.name: flcc
params.desc: Extracted-case design-variable array (one source's ``FlCc``, typically for a single CADGroup).

params.name: design_vars
params.desc: Column names in ``reference_df`` holding the design-variable values, in the same order as the columns of ``flcc``.

params.name: reference_df
params.desc: The DataFrame to search (e.g. a source's ``df_state`` or a ``get_df_metrics()`` result).

params.name: decimals
params.desc: Rounding precision for the identity match — see ``dedup_decimals`` in :meth:`merge_datasets`.

params.name: context
params.desc: Human-readable description of ``reference_df``, used only in error messages (e.g. ``"df_state of source 0"``).

returns.desc: ``len(flcc)`` rows of ``reference_df``, reindexed (0..n-1) to match ``flcc``'s case order exactly.

raises.desc: If ``reference_df`` is empty or missing one of ``design_vars`` as a column; if an extracted case in ``flcc`` has **no** matching row in ``reference_df`` (the case was extracted but is absent from this table — a genuine inconsistency); or if it has **more than one** matching row (the case cannot be unambiguously identified in ``reference_df`` at the requested precision).

text_sections.title: Examples
text_sections.text:
::

    matched_state = FRODO._match_rows_by_identity(
        flcc=db.data_dict['CADGroup_3']['FlCc'],
        design_vars=['AoA', 'Mach'],
        reference_df=db.df_state,
        decimals=8,
        context="df_state of source 0",
    )
    assert len(matched_state) == db.data_dict['CADGroup_3']['FlCc'].shape[0]

methods.name: merge_datasets
methods.signature: merge_datasets(root_dir: str, name: Optional[str], sources: list, new_group_id: str, method: str = 'idw', k: int = 4, mesh_ref: int = 0, cache: bool = True, get_df_metrics_attr: Optional[dict] = None, dedup_decimals: int = 8)

doc.summary: Merge multiple FRODO datasets into a single unified one.
doc.description:
Interpolates all source meshes onto a common reference mesh and
concatenates the ``FlCc`` arrays of every source, then rebuilds
``df_cases`` (and, when applicable to the format, ``df_state`` and
``df_post``) so that they describe **exactly** the cases that were
actually extracted into the sources (i.e. the rows already present
in each source's ``data_dict[...]['FlCc']``) — never the full set
of cases merely *defined* in a source's ``df_cases`` / ``df_state``.

params.name: root_dir
params.desc: Output root directory for the merged dataset.

params.name: name
params.desc: Name of the merged dataset. If None, defaults to 'FRODO_Merged'.

params.name: sources
params.desc: (FRODO_instance, CADGroupID) pairs to merge. Example: ``[(db1, '3'), (db2, '3_fine')]``.

params.name: new_group_id
params.desc: CADGroupID assigned to the merged group in the output.

params.name: method
params.desc: Mesh interpolation method. Supported: 'idw'. Default 'idw'.

params.name: k
params.desc: Nearest neighbours for IDW. Default 4.

params.name: mesh_ref
params.desc: Index of the source used as reference mesh. Default 0.

params.name: cache
params.desc: Cache KDTree / interpolation results between sources.

params.name: get_df_metrics_attr
params.desc: Keyword arguments for ``db.residuals.get_df_metrics()``. Required for format 'CODA'; must be left empty for any other format (an explicit ``ValueError`` is raised otherwise, so that non-CODA formats never accidentally depend on it).

params.name: dedup_decimals
params.desc: Number of decimal places used to round design-variable values when (a) checking that no case is duplicated across sources and (b) matching an extracted case (a row of ``FlCc``) back to its row in a source's ``df_state`` / ``get_df_metrics()`` result. Default 8 (matches the precision previously used, implicitly, for case deduplication).

returns.desc: A new FRODO instance whose ``metadata['df_cases']`` and, when applicable, ``df_state`` describe exactly the merged cases, in the same order as ``data_dict['CADGroup_<new_group_id>']['FlCc']``. For CODA, a matching ``df_post`` is additionally computed and saved to ``<root_dir>/metadata/df_post.csv``.

raises.desc: If fewer than two sources are given; if sources do not share the same format; if ``mesh_ref`` is not a valid index into ``sources``; if ``FlCc`` arrays have incompatible column counts; if sources declare inconsistent ``design_vars``; if the same physical case is found in more than one source; or if ``get_df_metrics_attr`` is given for a non-CODA format (or omitted for CODA).
If a requested CADGroup, or its ``FlCc``, is not present in a source's ``data_dict`` (i.e. ``extract_inputs()`` was not run for that group).

If an extracted case cannot be found, or cannot be unambiguously identified, in a source's ``df_state`` or ``get_df_metrics()`` result — this signals that ``df_state``/``df_post`` would otherwise end up misaligned with ``FlCc``.

If a source has no Sets class (``db.sets is None``), since mesh homogenisation goes through ``sets.interpolate_msh2msh``. This covers formats that store one mesh per case, such as CODA_SINGLE: merging them needs a strategy of its own, because :meth:`merge_datasets` assumes every source can be interpolated onto a single reference mesh.

text_sections.title: Design principles
text_sections.text:
* **``FlCc`` is the ground truth of "which cases are being
  merged".** A source's ``df_cases`` / ``df_state`` may describe
  more cases than were ever passed through ``extract_inputs()`` /
  ``extract_outputs()``; only the cases actually present in
  ``FlCc`` end up in the merged database.
* **No silent deduplication.** If the same physical case (by
  design-variable identity, see ``dedup_decimals``) appears in two
  different sources, :meth:`merge_datasets` raises ``ValueError``
  instead of picking one and discarding the other.
* **Format-agnostic core.** Case-set resolution, duplicate
  checking, mesh homogenisation, ``FlCc``/``Vars`` concatenation
  and ``df_cases`` construction do not depend on the source
  format. Only the ``df_post`` step (which uses
  ``CODAResiduals.get_df_metrics``) is CODA-specific, and is
  skipped entirely for other formats.
* **Alignment is guaranteed by construction, not by hoping.**
  ``df_state`` and ``df_post`` are built by matching each
  extracted case (a row of ``FlCc``) against the source table via
  design-variable identity (:meth:`_match_rows_by_identity`), so
  row ``i`` of ``FlCc``, ``df_cases``, ``df_state`` and ``df_post``
  always refers to the same physical case. If a case cannot be
  found (or found unambiguously) in one of these tables, that is
  treated as an error rather than a silently misaligned result.

text_sections.title: Side-effects
text_sections.text:
Mesh homogenisation temporarily adds an interpolated group
``CADGroup_<gid>_merge_tmp_<id>`` to the ``data_dict`` of every
non-reference source. Those groups are removed before returning,
also when an exception is raised, so the sources are left with
the same groups they had. The sources' own groups are never
modified or freed: call ``db.sets.remove_data()`` on them once
their memory is no longer needed.

text_sections.title: Examples
text_sections.text:
Merge two CODA sources whose cases were fully extracted::

    db_full = FRODO.merge_datasets(
        root_dir='/data/merged',
        name='merged_run',
        sources=[(db1, '3'), (db2, '3')],
        new_group_id='3_merged',
        get_df_metrics_attr={'var_metrics': ['CoefLift', 'CoefDrag']},
    )
    n = db_full.data_dict['CADGroup_3_merged']['FlCc'].shape[0]
    assert len(db_full.metadata['df_cases']) == n
    assert len(db_full.df_state) == n

Merge a NUMPY-format source pair (no ``get_df_metrics_attr``
needed, and no ``df_post`` is produced)::

    db_full = FRODO.merge_datasets(
        root_dir='/data/merged_numpy',
        name='merged_numpy',
        sources=[(db1, '3'), (db2, '3')],
        new_group_id='3_merged',
    )

doc.summary: Reassign pending Slurm jobs that are constrained to a failed node.
doc.description:
The cases are identified using the metadata stored in
``<root_dir>/metadata/cases_metadata.json`` and the working directory
reported by Slurm for each pending job.

The method:
    1. Reads the simulation metadata.
    2. Searches the user's PENDING Slurm jobs.
    3. Identifies jobs requesting ``broken_node``.

doc.summary: SAM – Simulations & Analytics Module
doc.description:
The steadfast companion to FRODO.

SAM is a utility module designed to assist with machine-learning
workflows, data transformation, and surrogate model preparation for
CFD simulations and other engineering data pipelines.

It is a **static namespace**: it is never instantiated, and every
entry point is reached as ``SAM.<Area>.<function>(...)``. Only
:class:`HDF5reader` is a real, instantiable object.

text_sections.title: Sub-modules
text_sections.text:
Gardener   – joint tensor assembly and normalisation for ML training.
HDF5reader – thin HDF5 file reader (numpy / torch output).
Backpack   – file utilities, mesh helpers, CSV/txt parsers.
Weapons    – point-cloud sorting, surface derivatives, GMM clustering,
             mesh-to-mesh interpolation.
DifferentialOperators – gradient / Jacobian / divergence on scattered
             points by moving least squares.
DictVisualizer – rich / networkx / pprint helpers for nested dicts.

text_sections.title: Examples
text_sections.text:
::

    from FotR import SAM

    SAM.DictVisualizer.rich_tree(db.data_dict)
    files = SAM.Backpack.pattern_pocket.find_files(path, endswith='.vtu')
    grad  = SAM.DifferentialOperators.gradient(X, f)

doc.description:
Gardener turns the per-group arrays a FRODO database produces
(coordinates, flight conditions, auxiliary features, solution
variables) into the single 2-D table a surrogate model expects.
The row layout is always::

    [x_coords | flight_conditions | aux_features | output_variables]

with one row per ``(point, case)`` pair, so a group of ``n_points``
nodes and ``n_cases`` cases yields ``n_points × n_cases`` rows.

Every builder returns a dict carrying both the raw ``'tensor'``
and its min-max normalised twin ``'scaled'``, together with the
``'mins'``/``'maxs'`` used. Passing those back as ``ref=`` is how
several datasets are put on a common scale — which
:meth:`concatenate_sets` relies on.

doc.description:
Backpack is the area the rest of the package leans on hardest:
readers call it to locate case files, parse CODA monitor logs and
build mesh connectivity. It groups four kinds of helper.

Filename patterns
    :class:`pattern_pocket` infers the common pattern behind a
    set of filenames or folder names, matches against it, and
    rebuilds concrete names from values. This is how readers turn
    a ``folder_fmt`` such as ``'aoa_{}_mach_{}'`` into the list of
    case directories.
Solver log parsing
    :meth:`read_cfd_times` and :meth:`get_df_from_csv` read CODA
    ``-out.txt`` wall times and monitor CSVs.
Mesh helpers
    :meth:`get_unified_connectivity`,
    :meth:`cell_connectivity_in_order` and
    :meth:`ensure_cell_data` work on PyVista grids;
    :meth:`read_horses_mesh_h5`, :meth:`read_horses_hsol_header`
    and :meth:`horses_expected_vars` cover the HORSES3D
    high-order formats, with :class:`HorsesLazyField` standing in
    for a field that has not been read yet.
Miscellaneous
    :meth:`eval_formula` evaluates an arithmetic expression
    through an AST parser instead of ``eval``;
    :meth:`same_columns` and :meth:`create_tensors_from_h5` are
    small array utilities.

text_sections.title: Notes
text_sections.text:
Two pattern implementations live side by side:
:class:`pattern_pocket` is the current one, and
:class:`pattern_pocket_ant` is its superseded predecessor, kept
only for callers that have not migrated. New code should use
:class:`pattern_pocket`.

text_sections.title: Warnings
text_sections.text:
``mesh.cells_dict`` **groups cells by element type**, so the
rows of the returned array follow that grouping and *not* the
mesh's original cell order.  Indexing the result with a mask
built in original cell order (e.g. from ``cell_data``) selects
the wrong rows on any mixed-type mesh.  Use
:meth:`cell_connectivity_in_order` when row order must match
the mesh's own cell order.

doc.summary: Padded connectivity of *mesh*, in the mesh's **own cell order**.
doc.description:
Unlike :meth:`get_unified_connectivity` — which walks
``cells_dict`` and therefore groups cells by element type —
this reads the raw VTK offset/connectivity arrays, so row ``i``
of the result always describes cell ``i`` of *mesh*.  That is
what makes it safe to combine with a boolean mask taken from
``mesh.cell_data`` (e.g. ``CADGroupID``).

Node indices refer to ``mesh.points``.  When *mesh* is the
result of ``extract_cells``, they therefore refer to the
extracted subset, already renumbered by PyVista.

Cells with fewer nodes than the maximum are padded with ``-1``.

returns.desc: Empty meshes yield shape ``(0, 0)``.

text_sections.text:
::

    celdas = mesh.extract_cells(mask)
    conec  = SAM.Backpack.cell_connectivity_in_order(celdas)
    # conec[i] are the node ids of celdas' cell i, into
    # celdas.points

methods.name: find_files
methods.signature: find_files(path: str, *, pattern=None, endswith=None, contains=None, not_contains=None, literal: bool = True, ignore_case: bool = False, sort: bool = True, verbose: bool = True)

doc.summary: Return files inside a directory whose filenames satisfy one or more filtering criteria.
doc.description:
Every filter accepts either a single string or any iterable of strings.
Filters are combined using logical **AND**, while multiple patterns inside
the same filter are combined using logical **OR**.

Patterns can be interpreted either as literal strings or as regular
expressions.

params.name: path
params.desc: Directory to search.

params.name: endswith
params.desc: Filename suffix(es). When ``literal=True`` this behaves similarly to ``str.endswith()``. When ``literal=False`` each pattern is interpreted as a regular expression that must finish at the end of the filename.

params.name: contains
params.desc: Pattern(s) that must appear somewhere in the filename.

params.name: not_contains
params.desc: Pattern(s) that must **not** appear in the filename.

params.name: literal
params.desc: Whether the supplied patterns are literal strings. * ``True`` → patterns are escaped with ``re.escape()``. * ``False`` → patterns are interpreted as regular expressions.

params.name: ignore_case
params.desc: Perform case-insensitive matching.

params.name: sort
params.desc: Sort the returned list alphabetically.

params.name: verbose
params.desc: Print a warning if no files are found.

returns.desc: Absolute paths of all matching files.

text_sections.title: Examples
text_sections.text:
Find every HDF5 file::

    files = SAM.Backpack.pattern_pocket.find_files(
        "/data",
        endswith=".h5"
    )

Find every VTU or HDF5 file::

    files = SAM.Backpack.pattern_pocket.find_files(
        "/data",
        endswith=[".vtu", ".h5"]
    )

Find every file containing "surface"::

    files = SAM.Backpack.pattern_pocket.find_files(
        "/data",
        contains="surface"
    )

Find every VTU file except backups::

    files = SAM.Backpack.pattern_pocket.find_files(
        "/data",
        endswith=".vtu",
        not_contains="_backup"
    )

Find every file ending with "_p<number>.hsol"::

    files = SAM.Backpack.pattern_pocket.find_files(
        "/data",
        endswith=r"_p\d+\.hsol",
        literal=False
    )

Find files whose name contains either Mach 0.7 or Mach 0.8::

    files = SAM.Backpack.pattern_pocket.find_files(
        "/data",
        contains=[
            r"mach_0\.7",
            r"mach_0\.8",
        ],
        literal=False
    )

Find every solution file regardless of case::

    files = SAM.Backpack.pattern_pocket.find_files(
        "/data",
        endswith=".H5",
        ignore_case=True

doc.summary: Geometry and field operations on unstructured point clouds.
doc.description:
The name covers four unrelated jobs that share one trait: they
all work on raw arrays of points and values, with no knowledge of
the database they came from.

Ordering
    CFD surface extractions arrive unordered, which makes a
    derivative along the surface meaningless. ``sort_by_centroid``,
    ``sort_lexsort``, ``sort_closed_curve_by_kdtree`` and
    ``sort_points_by_hull_projection`` produce the index order
    that makes the point sequence follow the geometry; which one
    to pick depends on whether the curve is closed and how
    irregular the sampling is.
Derivatives
    ``surface_derivative`` for first and second derivatives along
    a surface, ``finite_diff_derivative`` and
    ``finite_diff_derivative_Fornberg`` for arbitrarily spaced
    nodes, and ``compute_3dgrad_greengauss`` (with
    ``build_element_neighbors``) for a volume Green-Gauss
    gradient.
Clustering
    ``GMM`` fits a Gaussian mixture, optionally running a BIC/AIC
    sweep to choose the number of components, and writes out the
    figures and tables.
Interpolation
    The private ``_interpolate_*`` kernels (IDW, KD-tree IDW,
    ``griddata``, PyVista) are the engines behind
    ``sets.interpolate_msh2msh`` and ``sets.interpolate_vol2surf``.
    Call them through ``sets``, not directly.

methods.signature: surface_derivative(X, f, order: int = 1, min_ds: float = 1e-06, stencil_width: int = 1, poly_order: int = None)

doc.summary: Compute first- or second-order derivatives of a scalar field with respect to the arc length of a discrete curve or surface contour.
doc.description:
Two differentiation modes are available based on ``stencil_width``:

* ``stencil_width == 1``: standard finite-difference gradients
  via ``numpy.gradient`` / ``torch.gradient`` (O(h²) central).
* ``stencil_width > 1``: local polynomial regression (Savitzky-
  Golay style) evaluated analytically at the local centre, which
  reduces sensitivity to noise and handles irregular spacing.

params.name: X
params.desc: Ordered point coordinates defining the curve.

params.name: f
params.desc: Scalar field evaluated at the curve points. * 1-D ``(N,)``        – single snapshot, returns 1-D derivative. * 2-D ``(N, ncases)`` – multiple snapshots, returns 2-D derivative.

params.name: order
params.desc: Derivative order.  1 = first, 2 = second. Default 1.

params.name: min_ds
params.desc: Minimum arc-length increment; points closer than this are removed to avoid division-by-zero. Default 1e-6.

params.name: stencil_width
params.desc: Half-width of the local polynomial neighbourhood. ``stencil_width=1`` activates finite differences. Default 1.

params.name: poly_order
params.desc: Degree of the local polynomial (only used when ``stencil_width > 1``).  Must satisfy ``order ≤ poly_order ≤ 2 × stencil_width``. If None, set to ``min(max(order, 2), 2×stencil_width)``.

returns.type: np.ndarray or torch.Tensor matching the dtype and device of *f*.

text_sections.title: Examples
text_sections.text:
::

    # First derivative of Cp along arc length (numpy)
    dCp_ds = SAM.Weapons.surface_derivative(coords, Cp)

    # Second derivative with local polynomial smoothing
    d2Cp_ds2 = SAM.Weapons.surface_derivative(
        coords, Cp, order=2, stencil_width=5, poly_order=3
    )

doc.description:
These operators work on a point cloud with no connectivity: for
each point a local neighbourhood is gathered, a polynomial is
fitted to it by moving least squares, and the derivative is read
off the fitted coefficients. That makes them the tool of choice
when a mesh is unavailable or unreliable — which is the usual
situation for an extracted surface or a merged database.

The three public entry points share the same tuning parameters:
``radius`` (neighbourhood size; inferred when omitted),
``stencil_width`` (how many neighbours to fit through) and
``poly_order`` (degree of the local fit, 2 by default).

text_sections.title: Notes
text_sections.text:
All three build the same MLS operators through the private
``_build_gradient_operators``, so computing several of them over
the same cloud repeats that work; the cost is dominated by the
neighbour search.

    This mirrors the bookkeeping already performed by
    ``NUMPYReader._active_cases_idx`` and exists so that later code
    (e.g. a future Sets/Stats method) can map the *local* case axis

doc.summary: Build ``df_cases`` from the JSON's column dict, tolerating ragged bookkeeping columns.
doc.description:
``cases_metadata.json`` stores ``df_cases`` column-wise
(``orient='list'``). Adding a case to an existing study can leave a
bookkeeping column such as ``'exist'`` one entry short, and
``pd.DataFrame.from_dict`` then dies with ``ValueError: All arrays
must be of the same length`` — an opaque message, raised from deep
inside pandas and not caught by the JSON-loading guard around it.

The distinction that matters is what the column is *for*:

* **identity** columns (the design variables, ``'folder'``,
  ``'case_idx'``) define which case is which. If one of those is
  ragged the table cannot be trusted, so this raises with a message
  naming the offenders.
* every other column is bookkeeping. A ragged one is dropped, with
  a warning, instead of blocking the whole dataset.

params.name: raw
params.desc: ``{column: list_of_values}`` as read from the JSON.

returns.desc: Empty when *raw* is empty or not a dict.

raises.desc: If an identity column is shorter than the longest column.

methods.name: define_subset
methods.signature: define_subset(name: str, cases_idx: Union[list, tuple, range, int, str], overwrite: bool = False)

doc.summary: Define (or redefine) a named subset of cases from ``metadata['df_cases']``.
doc.description:
A subset is simply a stored, named list of ``df_cases`` row
positions.  Once defined, it can be referenced by name from
:meth:`extract_inputs`, :meth:`extract_outputs` and the CODA
residuals helpers that accept a ``subset`` argument, instead of
repeating the same ``cases_idx`` selection everywhere.

Case selection reuses the exact same normalisation logic already
used by ``cases_idx`` elsewhere in the reader
(``BaseReader._normalise_cases_idx``), so every value accepted by
``extract_inputs(cases_idx=...)`` today (``'all'``, an ``int``, a
``range``, or a ``list``/``tuple`` of ints) is also accepted here.

A case may belong to any number of subsets simultaneously: the
canonical storage is ``self.subsets``, a plain
``dict[str, list[int]]`` (not a single-valued column), which
removes the "one case, one label" limitation a boolean/categorical
column would impose. For inspection convenience this is mirrored,
read-only, onto a ``'subsets'`` column of ``metadata['df_cases']``
(one list of subset names per row) every time subsets change —
but that column is never read back to resolve a subset; it exists
purely so a human (or ``df_cases.head()``) can see membership at a
glance.

params.name: name
params.desc: Subset name.  Must be a non-empty string (surrounding whitespace is stripped).  Must not already exist unless ``overwrite=True``.

params.name: cases_idx
params.desc: Case selection, normalised via ``BaseReader._normalise_cases_idx`` against ``metadata['df_cases']``.

params.name: overwrite
params.desc: If True, silently replaces an existing subset with the same name. If False (default) and the name already exists, raises ``ValueError``.

returns.desc: The resolved, sorted list of case positions now stored under ``self.subsets[name]``.

raises.desc: If ``name`` is empty/whitespace-only, if it already exists and ``overwrite=False``, if ``cases_idx`` has an unsupported type or string value, or if the resolved selection is empty.
If ``cases_idx`` contains out-of-range positions.
If ``metadata['df_cases']`` is not available.

text_sections.title: Examples
text_sections.text:
Define a subset from an explicit list of case positions::

    db.define_subset(name='mach_07', cases_idx=[0, 1, 2])

Define a subset covering every case (rarely useful on its own,
but handy as a documented alias)::

    db.define_subset(name='every_case', cases_idx='all')

Redefine an existing subset after discovering more cases at that
Mach number::

    db.define_subset(
        name='mach_07', cases_idx=[0, 1, 2, 9], overwrite=True,
    )

A case can belong to more than one subset::

    db.define_subset(name='mach_07', cases_idx=[0, 1, 2])
    db.define_subset(name='low_aoa', cases_idx=[0, 3])
    print(db.list_subsets())
    # {'mach_07': [0, 1, 2], 'low_aoa': [0, 3]}

methods.name: _resolve_cases_idx
methods.signature: _resolve_cases_idx(cases_idx: Union[list, tuple, range, int, str] = 'all', subset: Union[str, None] = None)

doc.summary: Central case-selection resolver shared by every CODA method that accepts both a ``cases_idx`` and a ``subset`` argument.

params.name: cases_idx
params.desc: Same accepted values as ``BaseReader._normalise_cases_idx``. Default ``'all'``.

params.name: subset
params.desc: Name of a previously defined subset (see :meth:`define_subset`). Default None.

returns.desc: Resolved, validated list of case positions.

raises.desc: If ``subset`` is given but not a defined subset name.
If both ``subset`` and a non-default ``cases_idx`` are given, or if ``cases_idx`` itself is invalid (propagated from ``BaseReader._normalise_cases_idx``).
Propagated from ``BaseReader._normalise_cases_idx`` when ``cases_idx`` contains out-of-range positions.

text_sections.title: Semantics
text_sections.text:
* ``subset is None`` → behaves exactly like
  ``BaseReader._normalise_cases_idx(cases_idx, df_cases)``: the
  pre-existing ``cases_idx``-based selection, unchanged.
* ``subset`` is a valid subset name **and** ``cases_idx`` is left
  at its default value (``'all'``) → the subset's case positions
  are used, and ``cases_idx`` is silently ignored (it was never
  set to anything meaningful by the caller).
* ``subset`` is a valid subset name **and** ``cases_idx`` was
  explicitly set to something other than ``'all'`` → this is an
  unresolvable ambiguity (the caller asked for two different
  selections at once) and a ``ValueError`` is raised rather than
  silently picking one.

This makes the "subset wins, cases_idx is ignored" rule from the
module/class docs unambiguous: a default ``cases_idx='all'`` is
always compatible with any subset (there is nothing to conflict
with), while a real, non-default ``cases_idx`` together with a
``subset`` is rejected outright instead of guessing which one the
caller meant.

text_sections.title: Examples
text_sections.text:
Default behaviour, unchanged from before subsets existed::

    idx = reader._resolve_cases_idx(cases_idx=[0, 1, 2])
    idx = reader._resolve_cases_idx(cases_idx='all')

Selecting via a subset::

    reader.define_subset(name='mach_07', cases_idx=[0, 1, 2])
    idx = reader._resolve_cases_idx(subset='mach_07')
    # idx == [0, 1, 2]; cases_idx defaulted to 'all', so no conflict.

Conflicting selection — raises ``ValueError``::

    reader._resolve_cases_idx(cases_idx=[5, 6], subset='mach_07')

doc.summary: Walk ``outputs/`` and build ``sim_metadata`` and ``df_state``.
doc.description:
Matches folder names against the format pattern, maps each folder
to the closest entry in ``df_cases`` (by Euclidean distance in the
design-variable space), and counts available stages.

``df_state`` is fully rebuilt on every call by merging the
freshly-scanned execution state with ``metadata['df_cases']`` — it
is a derived view, never an independent source of case identity.
``metadata['df_cases']`` itself (and therefore any subset defined
via :meth:`define_subset`) is only mutated in place (e.g. the
``'folder'`` column is filled in) and survives repeated calls to
this method unchanged in row count/order.

    values, computation_times list.
self.df_state : pd.DataFrame
    One row per matched simulation.

doc.description:
``CODAReader.__init__`` keeps only the four format-agnostic keys of
``cases_metadata.json`` (``eq_type``, ``folder_fmt``,
``design_vars``, ``num_stages``) plus ``df_cases``. ``mesh_map`` is
specific to this format, so it is loaded here rather than widening
the parent's contract.

(empty when the file is missing, unparseable or carries no
``mesh_map``), so :meth:`parse_simulation_dirs` can rely on the key

the dataset moved, and a re-run with ``overwrite=False`` updates
``mesh_map`` without recopying — so resolution falls back in order:

1. the declared path, if it exists on disk;
2. a file with the declared basename inside the case folder;
3. any ``*.msh`` found in the case folder (:meth:`_find_case_mesh`).
